text:
TCP is connection-oriented and reliable; UDP is connectionless and best-effort.

**TCP:** Performs a handshake before data flows, then guarantees delivery by acknowledging and retransmitting lost packets. It delivers bytes in order, as a stream with no message boundaries, and applies flow control and congestion control. The cost is added latency, per-connection state, and head-of-line blocking, where one lost packet stalls everything behind it.

**UDP:** Sends independent datagrams with no handshake, no delivery or ordering guarantee, no retransmission, and no built-in congestion control. Message boundaries are preserved. It has an 8-byte header versus TCP's 20+, and lower latency.

Use TCP when you need correctness (HTTP/1.1 and 2, SSH, databases, email). Use UDP when timeliness matters more than completeness, or when you want to build your own reliability (DNS, VoIP, games, video streaming, and QUIC, which underlies HTTP/3 and implements reliability and congestion control on top of UDP).

Since UDP has no congestion control, applications that send heavily over it must implement their own or risk harming the network.
